1:
The opening word is read two ways. Robertson calls λοιπόν an accusative of general reference that "does not mean actual conclusion, but merely a colloquial expression pointing towards the end", and Ellicott agrees that "furthermore" misses it, since Paul "is not adding a further injunction, for he has as yet given none": the sense is "for the rest, then", a closing formula. Chrysostom reads it as substance: having dealt with what was pressing, Paul turns to "things that are perpetual, and which they ought continually to hear", so "finally" means "always and forever".

That two verbs are used strikes them as deliberate. Barnes notes the first is weaker, "we ask you", the second the ordinary word for earnest exhortation: "he might have commanded them — but kind exhortation usually accomplishes more than a command." Ellicott sharpens both: the marginal "request" is better, "a word of calm and friendly asking, implying that the person so addressed will recognise the propriety of complying", and "encourage" suits the second, "assuming that they are already so acting, but not with enough heart." Robertson notes the verb is not the classical "question" but the papyrus word for urgent request. Calvin makes the choice a rule of office: Paul beseeches "when he might rightfully enjoin", a modesty pastors should imitate, "that they may, if possible, allure people to kindness, rather than violently compel them." Chrysostom is struck harder: "he does not even speak of himself as of sufficient credit to exhort. And yet who was so worthy of credit? But he takes Christ along with him", as at 2 Corinthians 5:20.

"By the Lord Jesus" divides them. Barnes and Henry take it of authority, Paul speaking in Christ's name as his ambassador. Ellicott denies it is an adjuration at all, unlike Romans 12:1: it states the ground of the request, which is union — "we encourage you, on the strength of our union in the Lord Jesus." At verse 2 he presses it again: the Lord is not the messenger who carried the commandments but "the person by means of whose inspiration St. Paul was enabled to give such commandments." Henry draws the limit on apostolic authority: they were commissioned to teach what Christ commanded, "not to give forth commandments of their own", nor to act as lords over God's heritage — "nor should any do so that pretend to be their successors."

Ellicott finds a catechism inside "how ye ought to walk": the article makes it "the how", suggesting part of the apostolic tradition was a systematic moral code, "almost as if it were the title of a well-known book". Henry turns the phrase into an aphorism — "the apostle taught them how to walk, not how to talk."

On abounding, Chrysostom alone builds a structure. Virtue divides into declining from evil and doing good, and withdrawal from evil is no arrival but "a kind of path, and a beginning leading thereto". Things to be avoided are given "in the order of commandment", since doing them brings punishment and not doing them no praise; acts of virtue like giving away one's goods are not commanded but offered — "he that is able to receive, let him receive", Matthew 19:12. To abound is to pass beyond the limit of the commandments, "for as the earth ought not to bear only what is thrown upon it, so too ought the soul not to stop at those things which have been inculcated." Calvin takes the word as evidence, not aspiration: urging progress, Paul "intimates that they are already in the way". Henry adds that those who most excel others still fall short of perfection; Clarke removes the ceiling — God sets no bounds to the communications of his grace, "and as there are no bounds to the graces, so there should be none to the exercise of them."
3:
Whether "the will of God" here is decree or command divides Gill from Barnes. Gill takes it as both, beginning with "the will of his purpose and decree; for in the same decree that he wills the salvation of any by Jesus Christ, he also wills their sanctification", and adding the approving will and the will of command after. Barnes forbids that reading in terms: it "does not refer to the purpose or decree of God, and does not mean that he intended to make them holy", only that he requires holiness — "this text should not be brought as a proof that God intends to make his people holy." Ellicott puts it positively: "the mere conversion, justification, salvation of us are not the aim of God: He would have us holy." Calvin supplies the sacrificial image: renouncing the world and clearing ourselves of the flesh's pollutions, "we offer ourselves to God as if in sacrifice, for nothing can with propriety be offered to Him, but what is pure and holy."

Robertson explains why a new word was needed. ἁγιασμός is found only in the Greek Bible and in ecclesiastical writers, coined to displace an older term carrying "technical ideas of consecration to a god or goddess that did not include holiness in life": pagan religion "did not demand sexual purity of its devotees". Ellicott makes the point from the other side: to the Gentile mind adultery's wickedness was obvious, but "it was a novelty to be told that fornication was a 'deadly sin'" — which explains the odd company the prohibition keeps at Acts 15:20, and how Paul can praise these converts while correcting them here, in "compassionate consideration towards the ignorant and deceived." On the word's range they part: Clarke takes it to include all sorts of uncleanness, several manuscripts, versions and fathers accordingly adding "all", where Ellicott insists it "must be understood in its strict sense."

The vessel of verse 4 splits them four ways. Gill will not decide, "for the Jews call both by this name". Clarke leans to the wife, citing the weaker vessel of 1 Peter 3:7, and notes "a third sense which interpreters have put on the word, which I forbear to name." Robertson also inclines to the wife and draws his own moral: the man must acquire her "in sanctification and honour" — "there is no double standard here. When the husband comes to the marriage bed, he should come as a chaste man to a chaste wife." Barnes and Calvin take it of the body — Barnes because Paul directs the whole church, "and it is hardly probable that he confined his direction to those who had wives"; Calvin because he "addresses husbands and wives indiscriminately", every man having "his body as a house, as it were, in which he dwells." Henry agrees, calling the body the vessel of the soul.

Ellicott turns the best evidence for the wife against it. The reading would lay "an emphatic and binding veto upon celibacy"; it is no part of a religious man's duty "to know how to procure a wife"; and Peter's phrase cuts the other way, since calling the wife the weaker vessel implies the husband is one too. He then refines "body": not a receptacle but an instrument, "not dissociated from the man's personality, as in the fanciful Platonism of Philo, but almost identified with it."

At verse 5 Ellicott hears grammar doing moral work: the word usually rendered "passion" implies "something which befalls a man, something done to him", so the phrase means "not in the helpless passivity of concupiscence" — an attempted mastery which is really abandonment. Clarke refuses the usual comparison: some say "not like beasts", but the brute creation is "regular and consistent" here, so of the two the Gentiles "are the beasts; their own brutes are rational creatures when compared with them."
6:
What "defraud his brother in the matter" forbids is disputed. Gill reports the common reading — cheating in trade, false weights, a hint "the rather necessary, since Thessalonica was a place of great trade and business" — then rejects it, since the subject before and after is chastity, and takes the phrase of adultery, "or rather sodomitical practices". Clarke and Wesley confine it to the marriage bed, Wesley completing a list of three prohibitions: fornication at verse 3, inordinate affection within marriage at verse 5, and here breach of the marriage contract. Barnes will not narrow it: the adulterous sense is included, "but there is no reason why it should be confined to it", the Greek covering any attempt to deprive another of his rights, in property or in marriage. Calvin agrees and turns on Chrysostom, whose gloss of the two verbs as neighing after other men's wives he calls "too forced an exposition": Paul, having given his instance of lust, now teaches that righteous dealing with neighbours "is also a department of holiness". Ellicott and Robertson note only that Paul writes "the matter", not "any matter", chosen "for delicacy's sake".

Ellicott alone reads the grammar structurally: the clause is not parallel to abstaining and knowing but a final clause stating their purpose — "men are to be chaste and self-possessed, not only for their own salvation's sake, but in justice to their brethren." Where the earlier chapter had them love in order to become holy, "here they are to be holy for the sake of charity — a blessed action and reaction." On the avenger he is as precise: the vengeance is that of the Judgment Day, "not the natural retribution which carnal sin brings with it", so "the Lord" here means the Incarnate Son, "who has a special claim upon men's bodies." Robertson adds that the word is the papyrus term for a legal avenger. Calvin explains the vehemence: "such is the sluggishness of mankind, that, unless they are wounded to the quick, they are touched with no apprehension of God's judgment."

At verse 7 Robertson makes two prepositions carry the argument, one meaning on the basis of, the other within the sphere of. Ellicott presses the first — it implies "not so much the definite end to which we are invited, as the terms on which the invitation will still stand" — and corrects the second noun outright: "holiness is a mistranslation for sanctification. The process, not the quality, is meant." Clarke reads the verse as a defence of marriage rather than a caution against it, God being its institutor, though "the end of this and all the other callings of God to man is holiness". Calvin, after arguing from possession, turns on those who ridicule such instruction: "such persons must not be taught, but must be beaten with severe reproofs as with the stroke of a hammer."

The last verse turns on a letter. Clarke assembles the case for reading that God gave his Spirit not "unto us" but "unto you" — a long list of manuscripts and versions, with Clement, Didymus and Ambrosiaster. He builds a distinction on it: "it is one thing to receive a revelation from the Spirit of God; it is another thing to receive that Spirit to enable a man to live according to that revelation" — the first to the apostles alone, the second to all Christians. Ellicott goes further — "or more correctly into you", a Spirit sent to enter and dwell. Barnes, keeping "us", makes the verse mean something else: "this is a claim to inspiration." Calvin observes the variant and declines to choose. Robertson notes the verb for despising means to annul: "in order to justify their licentiousness they do not hesitate to set aside God." Wesley alone stops to admire the sentence — "what naked majesty of words! How oratorical, and yet with what great simplicity!"
9:
Chrysostom asks why the chief of all good things is introduced as though passed over, and answers that the disclaimer marks the duty as too necessary to need teaching — "for things that are very important are manifest to all" — and shames more effectively than admonition would. The paradox delights him: Paul "ought then to have been silent... But now by saying there is no need, he has done a greater thing, than if he had said it." Ellicott names the device: "a sweet rhetorical figure, by which men are encouraged to a duty in which they are not perfect, by the praising of their imperfect attempts". His paraphrase of the underlying sense is blunter: "your charity is hardly catholic enough, nor have you exercised it with sufficient sobriety and thrift."

Robertson notes that in profane Greek and the Septuagint the word means love of those kin by blood, in the New Testament kinship in the love of Christ. Ellicott calls it "pretty nearly what we call 'Church feeling'" and refuses to rank it high: "in itself, it is not the most exalted of graces, being to some extent the outcome of community of interests" — hence Peter makes it a means to the higher grace of charity. The rarer word is "taught of God", found nowhere else. Barnes says what it is not — "not of the nature of revelation or inspiration" — but the secret teaching of providence, conscience and the Spirit, loving the brethren being "one of the first, the elementary effects of religion on the soul". Calvin says the same in his own idiom: love was "engraven upon their hearts, so that there was no need of letters written on paper". Ellicott hears Paul change course mid-sentence, beginning "ye yourselves know without any instruction" and substituting its source.

Where the ambition of verse 11 attaches is disputed; most take it with what follows, as ambition to be quiet. Calvin detaches it and joins it to the love of verse 10 — "a sacred emulation, that they may strive among themselves in mutual affection", or rather that each strive to conquer himself: "this is the best emulation, when each one strives to overcome himself in doing good." The others keep the paradox. Ellicott calls "make it your ambition to keep quiet" a strong oxymoron, aimed at men whose ambition had been "to make a stir among the Churches"; Gill imagines a contest for "the honour of being the quietest person in the community"; Barnes translates it "to make it a point of honour" and concludes that "no Christian should be engaged in a mob"; Robertson, that the ambition is to do good — "a preacher devoid of ambition lacks power".

What the disorder was they read differently. Clarke sees individuals — "idle, tattling people" who "under the pretense of religion, gadded about from house to house", procuring their bread by religious gossiping — and concludes that "an idle person, though able to discourse like an angel, or pray like an apostle, cannot be a Christian." Ellicott makes it corporate: not merely was each man to do his own work, but "the whole Church was to refrain from interfering ostentatiously with other Churches", these Thessalonians having organised so busily abroad that their own industry suffered. He and Robertson trace the restlessness to a misapprehension about the Advent, though Ellicott admits "proof is impossible". Calvin sets the remedy in vocation: the husbandman at his labours, the workman at his occupation, "and in this way every one keeps within his own limits". On the hands, Ellicott infers most of these Christians were artisans, Robertson that Paul "gave a new dignity to manual labour by precept and example". Barnes holds that religion "makes no one idle, and it countenances idleness in no one", and that the rule applied universally "would speedily put an end to slavery".
13:
Four of them correct the pronoun: the reading is "we would not have you ignorant", Paul still speaking for his companions. Clarke calls it "undoubtedly the true reading" and Gill reports it from the Alexandrian copy.

What the ignorance was they reconstruct differently. Chrysostom denies it was disbelief in the resurrection: they did not disbelieve, "but nevertheless bewailed", and men enquiring about times and seasons knew the doctrine well enough. He notes Paul's method changing with the audience: at Corinth he argued from reasonings, but here "he introduces nothing from reasonings, because they were docile." Calvin reasons the same way: the hope had not been "torn up among the Thessalonians by profane men, as had taken place at Corinth", though it may not have been fixed enough to keep out "something of the old superstition". Barnes, following Koppe, proposes two causes: some doubting the resurrection outright, others believing the dead would rise but long after the living were taken to glory, remaining "always in a condition inferior to them."

The sleeping divides their methods sharply. Ellicott insists the image is "a mere metaphor... therefore no doctrine can be deduced with precision from it": one cannot say that only the body sleeps and not the soul, nor that the soul sleeps while the body lies in the grave. Calvin draws exactly the inference Ellicott forbids: the term "refers not to the soul, but to the body, for the dead body lies in the tomb, as in a couch, until God raise up the man. Those, therefore, act a foolish part, who infer from this that souls sleep." Robertson and Ellicott agree on the tense against the later manuscripts: the participle is present, not perfect, giving "the idea of repetition, from time to time fall asleep" — "the grief renewed itself over each successive death-bed."

Whether any sorrow is permitted divides them again. Ellicott takes the prohibition absolutely: Paul "wants them not to sorrow at all over the dead", not merely less than the heathen, since "to Christians, who have a hope, and such a hope, death ought to have no sorrows"; the Prayer-book burial office is "as joyous as the Eucharistic Office itself." Calvin will not have it: Paul "does not forbid us altogether to mourn, but requires moderation in our mourning", and those who use the text to establish "Stoical indifference, that is, an iron hardness, will find nothing of this nature in Paul's words" — "it is one thing to bridle our grief, that it may be made subject to God, and quite another thing to harden one's self so as to be like stones, by casting away human feelings." Barnes agrees that religion "does not blunt the sensibility of the soul", Jesus having wept at Lazarus's grave; Wesley puts it most economically — Christianity "neither takes away nor embitters, but sweetly tempers, that most refined of all affections, our desire of or love to the dead."

On the hopelessness of the others, Robertson cites the tombstone inscriptions — a few pagans clung to hope, most had none — and Barnes the funerals: hired pipers, women engaged to howl, dust cast on the head.

Verse 14 gives Chrysostom his opening against those who denied the flesh: "if He did not assume Flesh, neither did He die. If He did not die, neither did He rise again." He rejects the reading that makes "through Jesus" mean the baptized, since "Jesus did not fall asleep through Baptism", concluding that Paul discourses "not of a general Resurrection, but of a partial one." Barnes reads "sleep in Jesus" as cause, not circumstance, and corrects the last clause: God will bring them not down from heaven with the Saviour but up from their graves. Clarke calls it a new discovery that the dead rise first, and so "in some measure, have the preference and advantage of such as shall then be found alive."
15:
"By the word of the Lord" is claimed four ways. Ellicott makes it absolute — "a most direct claim to plenary inspiration", meaning neither "according to certain words which Christ spoke" nor "by means of a revelation from the Lord to me" but "by way of a divine revelation". Barnes reports the suggestion that Paul alludes to Matthew 24:30, but denies an exclusive reference, since details appear here that are absent there, and concludes for a private communication. Calvin takes the opposite road: the phrase probably means what was drawn from Christ's own discourses, since the point was better established by reporting "those things that had been uttered by Christ's own mouth" — "we are not the first witnesses of the resurrection, but instead of this the Master himself declared it." Robertson admits ignorance: Jesus may have spoken so without the saying being preserved. Chrysostom sets it against prophetic convention: the prophets wrote "thus saith the Lord", but Paul, "not having seen Him sitting, but having Christ speaking in himself", writes "do ye seek a proof of Christ speaking in me?" — and where his other teaching came by the Spirit, this "he heard even expressly from God".

Whether Paul expected to be among the living divides them too. Clarke denies it and makes the denial doctrinal: the pronoun includes neither Paul nor his readers, since "it is impossible that a man, under so direct an influence of the Holy Spirit, should be permitted to make such a mistake." Ellicott is candid: "there is not the least necessity for supposing that St. Paul confidently expected the Advent before his death. Very likely he did, but it cannot be proved from this passage." He explains the first person as Paul identifying with an expectation his converts already held; besides, "it is far easier to imagine himself among the quick than among the dead at that moment." Robertson notes only that Paul "was alive, not dead, when he wrote." Calvin makes the usage pastoral: it holds believers in suspense "that they may not promise themselves some particular time".

Two of them stop to rescue an English verb. "Prevent" means to precede, as Barnes shows from Job and the Psalms and Clarke from Hesychius: the living shall not "anticipate glory before the dead in Christ". Robertson adds that the Greek double negative is the strongest; Ellicott paraphrases, "we shall certainly not get the start of them that sleep; if anything, we shall be behind them." Ellicott alone reconstructs the fear: they dreaded that the kingdom's highest glories would be engrossed by the living, which made them "not only sorry for their dead friends, but also reluctant to die themselves."

Gill insists the descent is personal — not by proxy, "not by the ministry of angels, as on Mount Sinai", but in soul and body. The shout draws out the lexicographers. Barnes finds the word used of sailors at the oar, of soldiers rushing to battle, of a huntsman calling his dogs, and infers the Lord does not utter it but is attended by it. Ellicott, hearing a captain's or boatswain's command, refuses to speculate, since "it is not necessary to inquire what the command may be, or to whom issued" — the point is the noise in the midst of which the Lord descends. Clarke supplies the words anyway — "Arise, ye dead, and come to judgment" — and lays out a nine-stage order, refusing to borrow from poets "because I cannot trust to their correctness." Cyril puts the same proclamation in the archangel's mouth — "Arise to meet the Lord" — adding that "fearful will be that descent of our Master." Barnes notes that the noun lacks the article and could be rendered "an archangel", and that its voice cannot be what raises the dead, since that office belongs to the voice of the Son of God.
17:
"Then" is made to carry a good deal. Robertson calls it "the next step, not the identical time, but immediately afterwards", and Barnes agrees it marks succession, not simultaneity, allowing a momentary interval for the change of the living — but presses further, holding the succession close enough "to exclude the idea of a long interval in which other important transactions would occur, such as would be involved in a long personal reign of the Redeemer on earth."

The seizing verb interests Barnes most. It "implies the application of external force or power": not any capacity of ascending the saints possess, nor an effort of their will — witness the violent taking the kingdom by force, or the Spirit catching away Philip. It implies no reluctance, only that power is needed. On the clouds he leaves the question open: the Greek lacks the article, so the saints may ascend "in such grouping as to resemble clouds". Robertson keeps it simpler, an old verb "to seize, to carry off", the rapture of risen and changed being "a glorious climax to Paul's argument of consolation". Ellicott names it "our Assumption" and disposes of the physics briskly — "clouds and air will be support enough for material so immaterial."

Where the judgment happens is the sharpest disagreement. Barnes infers from "in the air" that the Lord "would not descend to the earth, but would remain at a distance from it in the air, where the great transactions of the judgment will occur", since "the world would not be spacious enough to contain all the assembled living and dead". Ellicott reads the phrase in the opposite direction. The word properly means the lower atmosphere where the powers of darkness reign, but here stands merely in contrast with the ground and means "on the way from Heaven whence He comes, of course not to dwell there, but to accompany Him to His Judgment-seat on the earth." He supports it with Chrysostom's image — "when the King cometh into a city, they that are honourable proceed forth to meet him, but the guilty await their judge within." Wesley reads a division of levels, the wicked beneath while the righteous, absolved, sit as assessors with their Lord. Robertson will not settle the sequel: "whether with a return to earth or with an immediate departure for heaven Paul does not say."

Two of them turn the last clause against millenarianism. Calvin says the promise refutes "the reveries of Origen and of the Chiliasts", since believers gathered into one kingdom have a life no more ending than Christ's: "to assign to Christ a thousand years, so that he would afterwards cease to reign, were too horrible to be made mention of." Barnes says flatly that "there is no intimation here of a personal reign of Christ upon the earth".

On the closing exhortation Ellicott prefers "in these words" to "with", taking it as a prescription: "repeat these very words to one another, and you will find the comfort." Gill enumerates the doctrines: the saints do not cease to be but sleep in Jesus, their bodies are his care, they will be with him as soon as the living, and part no more. Clarke alone finds the command strange: "comfort a man with the information that he is going to appear before the judgment-seat of God! Who can feel comfort from these words?" Only the man whose sins are blotted out, he answers, or who hungers after righteousness: "it is impossible that thou shouldst be taken away in thy sins, while mourning after the salvation of God." Barnes closes on what the passage owes to revelation: it holds a truth "to be found in no heathen classic writer", reason having "never dared to conjecture that such scenes would occur"; and against the fear of dying he sets Paul's figure — "is the slumbering of an infant an object of terror?"
